title: Responsive Web Design
subtitle: Build websites that adapt to phones, tablets and computers
description: Learn how to make web pages fit different screen sizes using the viewport meta tag, flexible layouts, responsive images and CSS media queries.

blocks.title: 1. What Is Responsive Web Design?
blocks.text: Responsive Web Design means creating websites that adapt to different screen sizes. A website should remain readable and usable on a phone, tablet or computer. Instead of designing for only one screen width, we use flexible layouts, suitable text sizes, responsive images and CSS media queries. For example, three course cards may appear in one row on a computer but stack vertically on a small phone. The goal is not simply to make everything smaller. It is to make the content fit comfortably and remain easy to use.

blocks.title: Example 1: Set Up the Viewport
blocks.code:
Welcome to Code Academy

Learn to code on any device.
blocks.explanation: The viewport meta tag tells mobile browsers to use the device's viewport width when laying out the page. Without it, a phone may render the page as if it were a much wider desktop page and scale it down.

blocks.question: Why is the viewport meta tag important for responsive websites?
options: It automatically creates a navigation menu.
It helps the browser use the device's viewport width for page layout.
It changes every font to a smaller size.
It automatically creates CSS media queries.
blocks.explanation: The viewport meta tag helps mobile browsers lay out the page using the device's viewport width. It does not automatically create menus, resize all fonts or write media queries.

blocks.title: 2. Use Flexible Layouts
blocks.text: Fixed widths can cause problems on small screens. For example, a container with width: 900px may overflow a phone screen. Using width: 100% lets an element fill the width available from its containing block, while max-width limits how wide it can grow. The box-sizing: border-box rule makes an element's declared width include its padding and border, which can make sizing easier to manage. Flexbox and Grid are also useful for responsive layouts because they can arrange content according to the available space. Remember that width: 100% does not mean the element will always fit if other constraints or overflowing content are present.

blocks.explanation: width: 100% allows the container to use the available width. max-width: 900px prevents it from growing beyond 900px, and margin: 0 auto centers it when extra horizontal space is available.

blocks.question: What is the main purpose of max-width: 900px on a container with width: 100%?
options: It makes the container always 900px wide.
It prevents the container from growing beyond 900px.
It forces the container to use 90% of the screen.
It makes the container visible only on desktop screens.
blocks.explanation: width: 100% lets the container fill the available width, while max-width: 900px limits its maximum width to 900px.

blocks.title: 3. Media Queries: Change the Layout
blocks.text: A CSS media query applies styles when a specified condition is met. For example, @media (max-width: 600px) applies its styles when the viewport width is 600px or less. You can use it to stack navigation links, reduce spacing or change a multi-column layout into one column. The breakpoint should be chosen based on when your content needs a different layout, not just because a particular device exists. Styles outside the media query continue to apply unless the query overrides them. This lets you define a normal layout and make targeted changes for smaller or larger screens.

blocks.question: When does @media (max-width: 600px) apply?
options: Only when the viewport is exactly 600px wide.
When the viewport is 600px wide or narrower.
Only when the viewport is wider than 600px.
Whenever the page contains an image.
blocks.explanation: max-width: 600px includes viewport widths of 600px and below. It is not limited to exactly 600px.

blocks.title: 4. Responsive Images and Text
blocks.text: Images that are wider than their containers can cause horizontal scrolling. A common solution is max-width: 100% and height: auto. This lets an image shrink to fit its containing block while preserving its natural aspect ratio. For text, use readable font sizes and line heights. Relative units such as rem can help text scale consistently with the root font size. Avoid setting large fixed widths on text containers, and make sure long words or links do not force the page wider than the screen. Responsive design is about comfortable reading and interaction, not just fitting everything onto the screen.

blocks.question: Which CSS rule allows an image to shrink to fit its container while preserving its aspect ratio?
options: width: 900px; height: 900px;
max-width: 100%; height: auto;
min-width: 1000px; height: auto;
width: 100vw; height: 100vh;
blocks.explanation: max-width: 100% limits the image to the width available in its container, and height: auto preserves its natural aspect ratio.

blocks.title: 5. Mobile-First Design
blocks.text: Mobile-first design means starting with styles for small screens and then adding enhancements for wider screens. This approach encourages you to focus on essential content, clear spacing and simple navigation first. For example, you might begin with one column and add three columns when the viewport becomes wider. A min-width media query is commonly used for these wider-screen enhancements. Mobile-first is a design strategy, not a requirement that every website must use. The best approach is the one that keeps your content clear and usable at every relevant screen size. Always test your layout rather than assuming it will work.

blocks.question: Which example best represents a mobile-first approach?
options: Start with a three-column layout and never change it.
Start with a one-column layout, then add columns at wider breakpoints.
Hide all content on small screens.
Use fixed pixel widths for every element.
blocks.explanation: Mobile-first begins with a layout suitable for smaller screens, then enhances it for wider screens, often using min-width media queries.

blocks.title: 6. Quick Practice and Summary
blocks.text: You now know the foundations of Responsive Web Design. Use the viewport meta tag so mobile browsers can lay out pages at the intended device width. Prefer flexible widths and sensible max-width limits over unnecessarily large fixed widths. Use Grid or Flexbox to arrange content, media queries to adjust layouts at selected breakpoints, and max-width: 100% with height: auto for responsive images. Mobile-first design is a useful strategy when it suits your project. For practice, create a page with three course cards, make them stack on small screens, and add an image that stays inside its container. Test the page at different widths and check for horizontal scrolling, unreadable text and links that are difficult to tap. A responsive website should remain clear and usable, not merely look smaller.

blocks.question: A website looks fine on a computer but causes horizontal scrolling on a phone. Which is the best first step?
options: Inspect fixed widths, oversized content and the viewport setup.
Remove every media query from the stylesheet.
Set every element to position: absolute.
Increase all fixed widths so the layout has more room.
blocks.explanation: Fixed widths, oversized images or long content can cause overflow. Check those issues and confirm the viewport meta tag is present before choosing an appropriate responsive fix.

blocks.question: What is the main purpose of responsive web design?
options: To make every screen display exactly the same fixed layout.
To adapt the layout and content so the website remains usable across screen sizes.
To replace HTML with CSS.
To make every image fill the entire screen.
blocks.explanation: Responsive web design adapts layouts and content to different screen sizes while keeping the website readable and usable.
